explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. David is asking the opposite. He says, "What have I done? What is my iniquity? How have I sinned against your father, that he wants to take my life?" (1 Samuel 20:1). A man who knew his crime wouldn't be asking for the list. David is confused and scared, and he runs to Jonathan, Saul's son, with his questions.

Right, friend. David doesn't say he knows what he did. He asks Jonathan, "What have I done? What is my iniquity? How have I sinned against your father, that he wants to take my life?" (1 Samuel 20:1). Those are questions, not a confession. I think David is just as lost as a man who gets a bill for something he never ordered.

explanations.answer: His father tells him everything great or small
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Jonathan gives, baker. He says, "my father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. So why would he hide this matter from me?" (1 Samuel 20:2). Jonathan figures he'd be in the loop. Hold onto that, because David is about to poke a hole in it.

explanations.answer: His father has already forgiven David
explanations.explanation: Jonathan never says anything about forgiveness here. The text doesn't give David any offense to forgive, since David is asking what he even did (1 Samuel 20:1). Jonathan's reason is that his father "does nothing, great or small, without telling me" (1 Samuel 20:2). He thinks the king can't keep a secret like this from him.

explanations.answer: His father needs David to lead the army
explanations.explanation: Good guess if you're thinking like a general, but that's not Jonathan's reason. He says, "my father does nothing, great or small, without telling me" (1 Samuel 20:2). His argument is about being in the loop, not about army needs. Jonathan trusts that if his dad were plotting, he'd hear about it.

Yes, grieved. David says Saul told himself, "Jonathan must not know of this, or he will be grieved" (1 Samuel 20:3). So the king keeps Jonathan out of it because Jonathan would hurt over it. That's the secret Jonathan didn't know he was missing.

Jealous is a fair guess with this much drama going on, but it's not the word. David quotes Saul saying Jonathan "will be grieved" (1 Samuel 20:3). That's about Jonathan's sadness over what happens to his friend. The text gives us grief, so that's the word.

Close to the neighborhood, but not the word, friend. David says Saul keeps it quiet "or he will be grieved" (1 Samuel 20:3). Embarrassed is about how you look. Grieved is about how much it hurts, and that's what Saul expects Jonathan to feel.

Hide it is. David says, "let me go and hide in the field until the third evening from now" (1 Samuel 20:5). The king's table is where David is supposed to be, so he picks an empty field instead. Not exactly a five-star dining upgrade.

David isn't going hunting, baker. He says, "let me go and hide in the field until the third evening from now" (1 Samuel 20:5). Hiding is the plan, and it's not a hobby. He's staying out of sight while Jonathan checks on Saul.

Praying is never a bad idea, but that's not the word in the text. David says he'll "hide in the field until the third evening from now" (1 Samuel 20:5). The point of the plan is to be missing from the table while Jonathan watches how Saul reacts.

explanations.answer: That his father has evil intentions
explanations.explanation: That's it. David says, "If he says, 'Good,' then your servant is safe, but if he is enraged, you will know he has evil intentions" (1 Samuel 20:7). It's a simple test with two possible reactions. Saul's temper becomes the answer.

explanations.answer: That his father just needs more time
explanations.explanation: Waiting it out isn't part of David's test. He says a rage means "you will know he has evil intentions" (1 Samuel 20:7). He isn't looking for a cooling-off period. A furious Saul is the sign, and it means danger.

explanations.answer: That his father feels insulted by David
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't go there, friend. David says that if Saul "is enraged, you will know he has evil intentions" (1 Samuel 20:7). It doesn't say Saul feels insulted. I think David just wants a clear sign about whether his life is in danger.

True, and notice how bold David gets. He says, "If there is iniquity in me, then kill me yourself; why should you bring me to your father?" (1 Samuel 20:8). He'd rather face Jonathan, his covenant friend, than be handed over to Saul. That's a man who trusts his friend and knows his own heart.

It's true, baker. David says, "If there is iniquity in me, then kill me yourself; why should you bring me to your father?" (1 Samuel 20:8). He's asking Jonathan not to hand him over to Saul. I think David is that sure he's done nothing wrong.

True. Jonathan asks, "If he is favorable toward you, will I not send for you and tell you?" (1 Samuel 20:12). Good news gets delivered, and so does bad news. Jonathan is promising David a report either way.

It's actually true, friend. Jonathan says, "If he is favorable toward you, will I not send for you and tell you?" (1 Samuel 20:12). He promises to send word if Saul is friendly. Nobody gets left guessing, which is more than I can say for most group chats.

explanations.answer: Tell David and send him away safely
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jonathan swears, "may the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if I do not tell you and send you on your way in safety" (1 Samuel 20:13). He takes it that seriously. He puts his own name on the line for David's safety.

explanations.answer: Bring David to plead with the king
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of the plan. Jonathan swears to "tell you and send you on your way in safety" (1 Samuel 20:13). Taking David to the king is exactly what David asked him not to do (1 Samuel 20:8). Jonathan's promise is to get him out safely.

explanations.answer: Stand guard over David's hiding place
explanations.explanation: Nice loyal idea, but it's not what Jonathan swears. He says he'll "tell you and send you on your way in safety" (1 Samuel 20:13). He promises to send David away, not to stand watch. A guard standing around would also give the hiding spot away.

True. Jonathan asks David, "do not ever cut off your loving devotion from my household—not even when the LORD cuts off every one of David's enemies from the face of the earth" (1 Samuel 20:15). Jonathan is thinking about his family's future, even when David's troubles are over. That's a friend planning ahead.

It's true, baker. Jonathan says, "do not ever cut off your loving devotion from my household—not even when the LORD cuts off every one of David's enemies from the face of the earth" (1 Samuel 20:15). He asks David to keep showing devotion to his family. Jonathan is looking down the road.

That's the reason the text gives. It says Jonathan "had David reaffirm his vow out of love for him, for Jonathan loved David as he loved himself" (1 Samuel 20:17). Love is the whole motive here. Not a trace of doubt in it.

The text points the other way, friend. It says Jonathan had David reaffirm his vow "out of love for him, for Jonathan loved David as he loved himself" (1 Samuel 20:17). Doubt isn't mentioned anywhere. It's love, plain and simple.

explanations.answer: Out of fear of his father
explanations.explanation: Saul is a scary man in this chapter, but that isn't why. The text says Jonathan did it "out of love for him, for Jonathan loved David as he loved himself" (1 Samuel 20:17). Love is the reason, not fear.

That's the one. Jonathan tells David to "remain beside the stone Ezel" (1 Samuel 20:19). It's the place David hid when the trouble began. Easy to find, which matters when your friend is shooting arrows.
Bethlehem is in the story, but only as David's cover story (1 Samuel 20:6). Jonathan tells David to "remain beside the stone Ezel" (1 Samuel 20:19). That's where David is to wait.
Not a tree this time, friend. Jonathan says, "remain beside the stone Ezel" (1 Samuel 20:19). It's a stone, and it's the place David hid when this trouble began.

Safe is right. Jonathan says to the boy, "Look, the arrows are on this side of you; bring them," and then tells David, "it is safe for you, and there is no danger" (1 Samuel 20:21). Arrows closer means come out. I'd have needed a diagram, but David gets it.

It's the reverse, baker. Jonathan says that if the arrows are on this side, "it is safe for you, and there is no danger" (1 Samuel 20:21). The warning signal is different. Arrows beyond the boy mean go (1 Samuel 20:22).
Nothing is forbidden here. Jonathan says the arrows on this side mean "it is safe for you, and there is no danger" (1 Samuel 20:21). It's an all-clear signal. David is welcome to come.

True. Jonathan says, "if I say to the young man, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then you must go, for the LORD has sent you away" (1 Samuel 20:22). That's the warning signal. Arrows farther out means David has to leave.

It's true, friend. Jonathan says, "if I say to the young man, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then you must go, for the LORD has sent you away" (1 Samuel 20:22). Arrows beyond the boy mean David must leave. Two signals, two meanings.

Yes. Saul thinks, "Something has happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean—surely he is unclean" (1 Samuel 20:26). So he keeps quiet that first day. He has a reason in his head, and it isn't the real one.

explanations.answer: Something made him too sick to come
explanations.explanation: Sick sounds reasonable, but it isn't what the text says. Saul thinks, "Something has happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean—surely he is unclean" (1 Samuel 20:26). That's why Saul says nothing that day.

explanations.answer: Something called him back to Ramah
explanations.explanation: Ramah is where David ran from (1 Samuel 20:1), but Saul doesn't guess that. He thinks, "Something has happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean—surely he is unclean" (1 Samuel 20:26). That's the reason Saul stays quiet on day one.

True. Jonathan tells Saul David "urgently requested my permission to go to Bethlehem" because "our clan is holding a sacrifice in the city" (1 Samuel 20:28-29). It's the story David asked him to tell (1 Samuel 20:6). Jonathan sticks to the plan.

It's true, baker. Jonathan answers Saul, "David urgently requested my permission to go to Bethlehem," and says the clan is holding a sacrifice (1 Samuel 20:28-29). That matches what David asked him to say (1 Samuel 20:6). Jonathan keeps his word.

Kingdom is the word. Saul says, "For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established" (1 Samuel 20:31). He's telling his own son that David stands in his way. Jonathan hears it right at the table.
Army is a decent guess, but not the word. Saul says, "neither you nor your kingdom shall be established" (1 Samuel 20:31). He's talking about the throne, not the troops.

Not quite, friend. Saul says, "For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established" (1 Samuel 20:31). The word is kingdom. Saul is worried about the crown.

It's the other way around, baker. Jonathan doesn't agree. He pushes back: "Why must he be put to death? What has he done?" (1 Samuel 20:32). He stands up to his father, and the very next verse shows what that costs him.
Right. Instead of agreeing, Jonathan asks, "Why must he be put to death? What has he done?" (1 Samuel 20:32). He questions the king to his face. That takes real nerve.

explanations.answer: He hurls his spear at Jonathan
explanations.explanation: Sadly, yes. The text says, "Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to kill him" (1 Samuel 20:33). I think this one hurts, because it's a father throwing a spear at his own son. That's when Jonathan knows his father is determined to kill David.

explanations.answer: He orders guards to seize Jonathan
explanations.explanation: No guards show up in this scene. The text says, "Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to kill him" (1 Samuel 20:33). It's a heavy moment. I think it hurts to read.

explanations.answer: He storms away from the table
explanations.explanation: It's Jonathan who leaves the table, not Saul (1 Samuel 20:34). Saul does something much worse first: "Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to kill him" (1 Samuel 20:33). That's a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: He's hurt by how his father treated David
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Jonathan "was grieved by his father's shameful treatment of David" (1 Samuel 20:34). He's angry too, but the grief is about David. He sits out the meal over it.

explanations.answer: He's too afraid to stay near his father
explanations.explanation: Fear isn't what the text gives. It says Jonathan "got up from the table in fierce anger" and "was grieved by his father's shameful treatment of David" (1 Samuel 20:34). He's hurting for his friend, and the verse says so.

explanations.answer: He's ashamed of covering for David
explanations.explanation: There's no shame in Jonathan here. The text says he "was grieved by his father's shameful treatment of David" (1 Samuel 20:34). The shame in this verse belongs to how Saul acted, not to Jonathan.
Beyond is right. "Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him" (1 Samuel 20:36). That's the signal he and David agreed on for "you must go" (1 Samuel 20:22). The boy just thinks it's target practice.

explanations.answer: On this side of the boy
explanations.explanation: That would have been the all-clear signal (1 Samuel 20:21), but it's not what happens. The text says "Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him" (1 Samuel 20:36). Beyond meant David must go (1 Samuel 20:22).
Behind Jonathan wouldn't send much of a message, baker. The text says the boy ran and "Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him" (1 Samuel 20:36). Past the boy was the signal. It told David to go.
Not true, friend. The text says, "the boy did not know anything; only Jonathan and David knew the arrangement" (1 Samuel 20:39). He just fetched an arrow. Nobody told him a thing.
Right. The text says, "the boy did not know anything; only Jonathan and David knew the arrangement" (1 Samuel 20:39). To him it was just an arrow to fetch. Only two men knew what it really meant.
Weep it is. They "kissed each other and wept together—though David wept more" (1 Samuel 20:41). This is a hard goodbye. I think there wasn't a dry eye on that field.
No laughing here, baker. The text says they "kissed each other and wept together—though David wept more" (1 Samuel 20:41). It's a heavy goodbye between two friends.
No songs in this scene, friend. The text says they "kissed each other and wept together—though David wept more" (1 Samuel 20:41). Weeping is the word. They're saying goodbye.

explanations.answer: Go in peace because of the oath they swore
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jonathan says, "Go in peace, for the two of us have sworn in the name of the LORD, saying, 'May the LORD be a witness between you and me, and between your descendants and mine forever'" (1 Samuel 20:42). He sends David off with peace and a promise. The oath goes with him.

explanations.answer: Stay hidden here until the danger passes
explanations.explanation: The signal told David to leave, not stay (1 Samuel 20:22). Jonathan says, "Go in peace, for the two of us have sworn in the name of the LORD" (1 Samuel 20:42). David gets up and departs.

explanations.answer: Come back to the king's table very soon
explanations.explanation: That's not the farewell, friend. Jonathan says, "Go in peace, for the two of us have sworn in the name of the LORD" (1 Samuel 20:42). With Saul throwing spears, the king's table isn't safe for David.
